primary_topics: Keynote address at the First Integrity and Human Rights Conference, January 27, 2009 -- chaired by Leila de Lima; co-speaker with Loida Nicolas-Lewis (Bisyon 2020; met CJP in NUSP college days)

Corruption metrics: World Bank data (control-of-corruption worsened from 45% in 1996 under Ramos to 22% in 2007 under GMA; Philippines edged out Indonesia as most corrupt in East Asia); Transparency International rankings (121st in 2006 → 131st in 2007 → 141st in 2008)

Human rights metrics: Karapatan documented 977 extra-judicial killings, 1,010 torture victims, 1,464 illegal arrests during the eight years of the Arroyo administration; CHR Chair de Lima on 'dismal' record

Two solutions: (1) strict enforcement of the Ethical Standards Law; (2) strengthen democratic institutions by demanding from officials faithful performance of constitutional and legal duties -- citizens' role is oversight, not substitution
sub_topics: Loida Nicolas-Lewis connection: 'She and I have been involved in nation-building since our college days as organizers and officers of the National Union of Students of the Philippines' -- the NUSP connection spanning decades
World Bank corruption data: from 45% in 1996 (Ramos) to 22% in 2007 (GMA); 'we edged out Indonesia for the dubious title of being the most corrupt nation in East Asia'

Transparency International rankings: Philippines ranked 121st (2006) → 131st (2007) → 141st (2008); 'well below that of Mongolia (102), Nigeria (115), Ethiopia and Indonesia (both tied at 126). Somalia, the notorious home of pirates in Africa, was rated the most corrupt at the 180th place'
Pulse Asia survey (same as SA111): GMA 42%, Marcos 35%, Estrada 16%, Ramos 5%, Aquino 1% as most corrupt; 71% business managers bribed
Karapatan documentation during eight Arroyo years: 977 victims of extra-judicial killings; 1,010 victims of torture; 1,464 victims of illegal arrest

Leaders' response: 'mostly rhetoric, evasiveness and finger-pointing, like calling TI biased and suggesting it had been bought by the opposition, or ignoring the World Bank reports, or proposing some kind of authoritarian rule'

Enough laws already: 'we have enough laws and enough democratic institutions to fight graft and to uphold human rights, like the Ombudsman and the Commission on Audit. What is needed is leadership by example by the President to stamp out graft, the Ombudsman's exercise of independence and diligence to prosecute monster scalawags, and the COA's dogged insistence on accountability'

Ethics call: 'let them return to ethics, to old-fashioned principles like integrity, humility, fidelity, patriotism and prudence. In our world of short cuts and make-believe, society has bastardized ethics into public relations techniques. Such duplicity is fundamentally flawed. Instead of being a beacon of success and happiness, pretension is really a source of anxiety and frustration.'

Two solutions: (1) strict enforcement of the Ethical Standards Law; (2) strengthen democratic institutions by demanding faithful performance of constitutional and legal duties; 'citizens' role is not to substitute for what our officials should be doing. The citizens' job is to perform oversight functions: to demand that only the most qualified are elected or appointed, and then to insist that these public officials perform their duties ethically, courageously and competently.'

stances.claim: The Philippines does not need new laws to fight corruption -- it needs the existing institutions (Ombudsman, COA) to actually perform their mandated functions. 'What is needed is leadership by example by the President to stamp out graft, the Ombudsman's exercise of independence and diligence to prosecute monster scalawags, and the COA's dogged insistence on accountability.' The problem is institutional dysfunction, not statutory insufficiency.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-dysfunction-not-statutory-gap argument: the existing legal toolkit is sufficient; the failure is in the will to use it

stances.claim: Society has 'bastardized ethics into public relations techniques' -- making the outward appearance of ethical compliance a substitute for genuine ethical behavior. 'Such duplicity is fundamentally flawed. Instead of being a beacon of success and happiness, pretension is really a source of anxiety and frustration.' This is CJP's most pointed critique of the governance culture under GMA.
stances.rhetorical_move: ethics-vs-PR-duplicity argument: the distinction between genuine ethics and performative ethics as the root diagnostic of the governance failure
stances.confidence: asserted as a normative cultural observation

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 27, 2009 as keynote at the First Integrity and Human Rights Conference -- chaired by Leila de Lima (CHR Chairperson); co-speakers include Loida Nicolas-Lewis (Bisyon 2020; 'She and I have been involved in nation-building since our college days as organizers and officers of NUSP') -- this address presents a data-driven indictment of the Arroyo administration's governance record. World Bank data: control of corruption fell from 45% in 1996 (Ramos) to 22% in 2007 (GMA) -- 'we edged out Indonesia for the dubious title of being the most corrupt nation in East Asia.' Transparency International ranked the Philippines 121st (2006) → 131st (2007) → 141st (2008), 'well below Mongolia (102), Nigeria (115), Ethiopia and Indonesia (both 126). Somalia, the notorious home of pirates in Africa, was rated the most corrupt at 180th place.' Pulse Asia: GMA 42% most corrupt; 71% of business managers bribed. Karapatan documented 977 EJKs, 1,010 torture victims, 1,464 illegal arrests across eight Arroyo years. CHR Chair de Lima: the record is 'dismal.' The response from leaders: 'mostly rhetoric, evasiveness and finger-pointing, like calling TI biased and suggesting it had been bought by the opposition.' CJP's diagnosis: 'we have enough laws and enough democratic institutions... What is needed is leadership by example by the President, the Ombudsman's exercise of independence and diligence, and the COA's dogged insistence on accountability.' The root problem: 'society has bastardized ethics into public relations techniques. Such duplicity is fundamentally flawed. Pretension is really a source of anxiety and frustration.' Two solutions: (1) strict enforcement of the Ethical Standards Law; (2) strengthen democratic institutions -- 'the citizens' job is to perform oversight functions: to demand that only the most qualified are elected or appointed, and then to insist that these public officials perform their duties ethically, courageously and competently.'
